How to raise a sourdough starter

A sourdough starter is a living culture of wild yeast and bacteria that you keep alive with regular feedings of flour and water. It is the heart of every naturally leavened loaf, and with a little patience anyone can raise one on a kitchen counter.

Mix equal weights of whole wheat flour and lukewarm water in a clean jar, cover it loosely and leave it somewhere warm. For the first days nothing much happens, and that is normal. Around day three you should see bubbles and smell something pleasantly sour.

From then on, discard most of the starter every day and feed what remains with fresh flour and water. After a week the starter doubles in size within a few hours of feeding, which tells you it is strong enough to leaven bread.

Keep the jar at around twenty-four degrees if you can. Colder kitchens slow the fermentation, hotter ones make the starter turn acidic faster. Both are fine, you only need to adjust how often you feed it.

Once the starter is active, store it in the fridge and feed it once a week. Take it out the evening before baking, feed it again and let it wake up overnight. In the morning it will be bubbly and ready to build the dough.
